summary:
Fire behaves differently in space. Without gravity, flames are weaker and rounder, smoke doesn’t rise, and some materials burn at lower oxygen levels than they do on Earth. NASA has run decades of fire experiments, but the results are scattered across a huge database (PSI) and thousands of papers (NTRS). And astronauts heading to the Moon will breathe air that’s very different from the ISS’s.

FLARE (Freefall Lab Analysis & Ranking Engine) is our answer. You pick a scenario, such as the ISS, a Moon base or a spacesuit, and it ranks the NASA experiments that best match those conditions. It summarizes what they found and sorts the takeaways into prevent, detect and suppress. Every claim points back to its source, and anything we’re estimating rather than measuring is labeled that way.

We built it because a material that passes fire tests for ISS air isn’t automatically safe in a Moon base, and the people deciding that shouldn’t have to dig through terabytes of data to find out.
details:
What it does: FLARE helps people make sense of NASA’s fire-in-space research. You choose a scenario (ISS, Moon base or spacesuit) and it ranks the experiments whose conditions (oxygen level, pressure, gravity, material) best match it. It summarizes what each one found and groups the takeaways into prevent, detect and suppress. Every claim links back to its NASA source, and anything we estimate rather than measure is labeled as an estimate.

Why it matters: A material that passes fire tests for ISS air isn’t automatically safe in a Moon base, which is planned to have more oxygen at lower pressure. The evidence exists, but it is spread across NASA’s PSI database and NTRS papers. We make it usable for safety decisions.

Data and tools: NASA PSI and NTRS reports (SAFFIRE, FLEX, BASS, SoFIE, LUCI and others). [Add your actual stack, e.g. Python, Next.js, the AI model you used.]

What’s creative: A source citation is required before any claim shows on screen, and the ranking explains why an experiment matched.

Future: Add new data as it arrives, such as LUCI and NASA’s planned FM2 Moon experiment.
